newsitem.title: FINLAND: YEAREND-FINLAND SEEN HEADED FOR STEADY 1997 GROWTH.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-FINLAND SEEN HEADED FOR STEADY 1997 GROWTH.

text.p: Previously sceptical economists now believe Finland is headed for steady economic growth, slow inflation and a healthy current account surplus in 1997.
Most research institutes, banks and brokerages have recently upgraded forecasts in line with the finance ministry's projections, which a few months ago were seen as too optimistic.

The mean of eight 1997 GDP growth forecasts made in the past two months is 3.5 percent in a range from 2.5 to 4.6 percent. This year, Finnish GDP is seen rising 2.5 percent after 4.2 percent growth in 1995.
"In a European perspective, the pace of Finnish growth will be good," said Risto Murto, chief economist at brokerage Erik Selin Finance.
Although slower than in Finland, growth elsewhere in Europe is expected to be sufficiently strong to keep Finnish exports on a sustained rising track, economists say.

Demand abroad for Finnish exports -- mainly paper, sawn goods, metal and engineering products, electrotechnical goods and chemicals -- combined with a strengthening boom in domestic consumption and a recovery in construction will fuel growth.
"Growth up to four or five percent is not impossible," said Kirsi Hokka, economist at brokerage Alfred Berg.

"The export outlook is good, consumption prospects are good and it looks like construction is really taking off," she said, but added her 3.5 percent growth forecast would stay unchanged at least until the first quarter of 1997.
Helped partly by a modest cut in 1997 income tax, private consumption is forecast to increase 3-4 percent. Real earnings will rise some 2.5 percent and consumer confidence is strong.
Ari Aaltonen, chief economist at bank Postipankki, sees "stable, accelerating and sustained growth".
The positive scenario, and growing confidence that Finland will be in the first wave to join EMU in 1999 should tighten the yield gap over benchmark German Bunds, economists say.

Aaltonen expects the 10-year bond yield gap over Bunds to narrow to 10-15 basis points by the end of 1997 while Murto at Erik Selin Finance sees it at 20-40 basis points, down from some 55 bps currently.
But Postipankki's forecast highlighted a key question dividing high and low 1997 GDP projections -- investment.
Forecasts for a rise in gross fixed capital formation range from just above two percent to 11 percent.
"To see strong growth in industrial investment we should already have heard of many corporate investment decisions. We haven't," Aaltonen said.
The industrial lobby warned late in November of a 16 percent fall in 1997 manufacturing industry investment over 1996.
Forecasting 2.1 percent 1997 investment growth, he said three percent GDP growth was the best Finland should expect.
"To reach five, or even four percent GDP growth would mean really stunning growth in private sector output," he said.
"Because of the savings programmes still in effect, the public sector, which accounts for about one quarter of GDP, will grow by at most one percent next year," he added.
Pellervo Economic Research Institute (PTT), ideologically close to the opposition Centre Party, said weak investment would keep 1997 GDP growth around 2.5 percent.

Social Democrat Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen's government and the central bank are too intent on putting Finland in shape for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), and fiscal and monetary policies are too austere, PTT said.
"As a result, growth is too slow to reduce unemployment, our society's overwhelmingly most difficult problem," PTT said.
Unemployment is an increasingly sensitive issue for the left-right-green coalition, which in April 1995 set as its top priority to halve the jobless rate to 8-9 percent by 1999.
Economic policy has been marked by social welfare spending cuts under the banner that healthier state finances will take interest rates lower, boost growth and create new jobs.
This policy yielded returns as Standard & Poor's on December 17 upgraded Finland's foreign currency debt rating to double-A from AA minus.
But while Finland is about to enter 1997 with long-term interest rates some three percentage points lower than two years ago, unemployment is still nearly unchanged.
In November, the jobless rate rose to 17.4 percent from 17.3 percent in October, the labour ministry said.
As worry spreads, even senior government party MPs have begun to doubt EMU-tuned policies and some SDP MPs have embraced PTT's remedy: further monetary policy easing.
PTT called for the Bank of Finland's tender rate to be cut more from its current 3.00 percent level irrespective of whether the German Bundesbank shaves its key rates.

Economists across the board agree that Finnish inflation will remain low. Many welcomed central bank governor Sirkka Hamalainen's assessment on December 11 that conditions for slow inflation over the next few years remained "very favourable".

Forecasts for the year-on-year rise in 1997 CPI range from one to 1.8 percent. Consumer prices rose 0.7 percent in November and the partly EU-harmonised CPI gauge -- a refined version of which will be decisive for EMU -- rose 1.4 percent.

But contrary to PTT, brokerage Davy Protos is calling for monetary tightening to underline the importance of keeping inflation in check and avoid the threat of overheating. It said Finnish GDP might even soar six percent next year.
PTT and Protos are at opposite ends of the range of GDP growth forecasts (2.5-4.6 pct) and also the furthest apart on the employment outlook for 1997.
PTT says unemployment will not fall below 16 percent -- 400,000 people -- while Protos sees a decline in the number of unemployed to 367,000, or 14.5 percent of the workforce.
Both agree with the mainstream that the current account will show a surplus in excess of 20 billion markka -- 3.5 percent of GDP -- next year. It was 15.4 billion markka in January-October.
